clinicalPearls: X-linked recessive 46,XY disorder of sex development caused by loss-of-function variants in the androgen receptor, producing complete androgen resistance.
External genitalia are phenotypically female with a short, blind-ending vagina, and there is no uterus or fallopian tubes because anti-Müllerian hormone acts normally.
Testes are present (intra-abdominal or inguinal) and secrete testosterone and anti-Müllerian hormone; neither Wolffian nor Müllerian derivatives are present.
Classic presentations are primary amenorrhoea with normal breast development in an adolescent, or bilateral inguinal herniae or labial masses containing testes in a phenotypically female child.
Breast development at puberty results from aromatisation of testosterone to oestrogen, but pubic and axillary hair is characteristically scant or absent.
Gender identity is almost always female and the sex of rearing is female.
Germ cell tumour risk (gonadoblastoma or seminoma) is low before puberty and rises thereafter, which informs the timing of gonadectomy versus surveillance.
After gonadectomy, oestrogen replacement and attention to bone health are needed, and vaginal length can often be increased by dilation rather than surgery.
reference.pathophysiology: Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome is an X-linked recessive 46,XY disorder of sex development caused by loss-of-function variants in the androgen receptor gene at Xq11-q12. The complete absence of functional androgen receptor signalling makes target tissues wholly unresponsive to testosterone and dihydrotestosterone despite normal or elevated androgen production by intra-abdominal or inguinal testes. Because anti-Müllerian hormone from Sertoli cells is produced and acts normally, the Müllerian derivatives (uterus, fallopian tubes and upper vagina) regress; because androgen action is required both for Wolffian development and for masculinisation of the external genitalia and urogenital sinus during intrauterine development, internal male ducts fail to form and the external genitalia develop along female lines with a short, blind-ending vagina. At puberty testicular testosterone is aromatised to oestrogen and, unopposed by androgen, produces breast development and a female habitus, while pubic and axillary hair is scant or absent and menstruation does not occur. The gonads carry a risk of germ cell malignancy, such as gonadoblastoma or seminoma, which is low in childhood and rises with age.
additionalDifferentials: Partial androgen insensitivity syndrome (with ambiguous genitalia)
Steroid 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency (which virilises at puberty)
Complete gonadal dysgenesis (Swyer syndrome, 46,XY) with streak gonads and a uterus
Müllerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome) in a 46,XX individual with normal hair and ovaries
additionalInvestigations: Serum testosterone in the normal or high male range, with raised luteinising hormone and oestradiol
Anti-Müllerian hormone or inhibin B as markers of testicular tissue
Pelvic ultrasound or MRI showing an absent uterus and locating the gonads
Gonadal imaging, with histology where indicated to assess tumour risk
redFlags: An inguinal hernia or labial mass in a phenotypically female infant, which should prompt examination for gonads and consideration of a disorder of sex development
Primary amenorrhoea with an absent uterus
A gonadal mass or rising tumour markers suggesting germ cell malignancy
Significant psychological distress at the time of diagnosis disclosure
Reduced bone density if oestrogen replacement after gonadectomy is inadequate
reference.prognosis: General health and female gender identity are excellent; individuals are infertile and, after gonadectomy, require oestrogen replacement and attention to bone health, and benefit from psychological and peer support.
pitfalls: Confusing complete androgen insensitivity with Müllerian agenesis: the karyotype, gonads and pubic hair distinguish them
Removing the gonads in early childhood when malignancy risk is low and endogenous puberty is beneficial, rather than individualising timing
Neglecting bone health and oestrogen replacement after gonadectomy
Insensitive or non-consensual disclosure of the karyotype and diagnosis, which can cause psychological harm
Assuming a uterus is present and expecting menstruation or fertility
references: Consensus statements on the management of disorders of sex development
Clinical genetics references on androgen insensitivity
